events.title: recomp/mdamiga: colours grouped by how much of the screen shows them; sprites behind plane B's cells with priority. The fifteen slots of a playfield went to the colours farthest apart, so a rare bright one took a slot and the dark ones a stage is mostly made of shared one (Thunder Force IV's Air-raid: a grey sky with black boxes where it should be black; the panels' black gone brown). Now a colour weighs what the cells drawn with its tiles come to, the slots are picked by distance times weight and moved to the middle of their colours three times, and a slot's colour is the weighted mean. Sprites without priority are cut by the pixels of plane B's cells with priority (the stage select's pictures, which showed whole over the panel). recomp host: RECOMP_POKE=ADDR:VAL,... holds bytes every frame (lives, so a scripted run plays through for the analysis)

events.title: agk port: scratch below the stack pointer goes to the layer's page. Thunder Force IV's DMA routine does movea.l sp,a0 and splits the length into bytes through -(a0) and (a0)+ without moving the stack; on the Amiga the layer's interrupts come at any time and their frame lands there (the length's low byte came back as $6C, the frame's vector offset: a transfer too long by that much ran over the game's empty tile, and cells of rubbish spread over both planes on a slow machine). recomp/mdamiga: the blitter's sprites are on again. What the blitter can copy it copies: a cell is written to chip RAM once by the CPU and handed on to the other bitmaps, all of that and the putting back of sprites done before the CPU writes cells, the sprites in a second go. The VDP's state held across the game's handlers includes what a DMA is set up with and is kept on the stack around each handler (they nest, and this game's first one never returns). Cell rows are gone through from where the last pass stopped and the planes take turns; a colour seen for the first time with no close slot is grouped soon. Debug: -DDBG_WATCH=addr says who writes that VRAM, the F1 dump takes the layer's marks and shadow. Stock A1200: the demo's logic at about 67%

events.title: recomp/mdamiga: the blitter draws the sprites, the bitplanes are fetched 64 bits at a time, planes taller than the bitmaps. The bitmaps' lines hold their four planes one after the other, so one blit cuts a sprite into plane A (its image and mask kept in chip RAM, made once) and one puts back what it covered from a copy of plane A without sprites; a picture's blits are a queue the blitter's interrupt works through and the picture is shown when the last is done, never begun again before the blank that shows it. Sprites behind cells with priority or across a change of line scroll are still drawn by hand. FMODE 3 with the scroll's two extra bits: the bitplanes take 15% of the bus instead of 53%. The window's bitmap is laid out as the playfields' are (no pointer moves on its lines). A plane of 64 or 128 cell rows is seen through the bitmap's 32, each bitmap row holding the plane row in view (Thunder Force IV's stages scroll up and down: rows of the wrong cells before). Colours are grouped again only when the fit got worse than the last grouping left it, each time after twice the wait. The layer's page and its cell move to fast RAM with the code. Stock A1200: the demo's logic at about 60% of full speed

events.title: recomp/mdamiga: the frame's fixed costs. The scroll geometry is worked out by runs of lines and once a picture, the copper list visits only the lines where a pointer doesn't carry on, a tile the game rewrites finds its cells through a list per tile instead of both name tables being read through, cells go to chip RAM four at a time, and a regrouping that changes nothing keeps the colour tables. agk port: word-offset tables behind a shared dispatcher (lea T,aX; bra to move.w (aX,dY),dZ; lea BASE,aW; jmp (aW,dZ)) are read, each entry a way in (Thunder Force IV's object states: one the analysis hadn't run was swallowed by its neighbour's patch); a routine takes its data from after the call only where those bytes were read as data. events.title: agk port: a stop says it is asleep. The byte after the layer's cell is set before each stop and cleared when the Amiga's interrupt entry gives the game an interrupt; an interrupt of the Amiga's own puts the game back into the stop only while it is set. The return address alone is the same just after a wake, so a copper interrupt landing between the game's handler and the next instruction sent Thunder Force IV back to sleep for good (frozen on a demo's GAME OVER or the ranking, depending on timing). events.title: agk port: a second game. Thunder Force IV matches the original on 7997 of 8000 frames on the host and reaches its first stage on the Amiga. What it needed: a stack from address 0 is the top of RAM; stop's interrupt mask is lowered and on the Amiga an interrupt the game didn't get puts it back to sleep; a call with its data after it keeps the old return address; rte is the 68000's (move (sp)+,sr; rts) and the Amiga's interrupt entry builds frames to match; tables of routines behind a base register and routine addresses stored as immediates are followed (14,000 to 42,000 instructions); old bytes that never ran are neither patched nor poisoned; $A10001 answers the region the header asks for. The checking build looks at the chips' events where the original's control flow was (Sonic 2 now matches on all 4000 frames) and has RECOMP_PORT_STOP and RECOMP_DUMP_AT; an unhandled exception on the Amiga is reported on the serial port

events.title: agk port: the game runs first and the picture is drawn in its waits. The loops where the game waits for an interrupt are found (a test of RAM and a branch back to it) and listed for the layer; the copper raises an interrupt every sixteen lines and, when it lands in one, the layer draws until the blank is near. The VDP's status reads in-blank while the game's vertical interrupt runs (Sonic 2's handler waited a frame for the flag when the Amiga delivered it late). DMA to video memory compared and copied in longs, scroll geometry only when its inputs change, tiles to planar through a table per palette line, whole sprite cells a tile row at a time. Stock A1200 with fast RAM, sound off: Emerald Hill's logic from about 30% of full speed to 70-90%. README: the Mega Drive port

events.title: agk port: the game's RAM and code can be moved, and the Amiga's loader moves them to fast RAM. The port is done a second time for a layout a megabyte on and every long that moved is listed (in the code and in the ROM image); the loader adds the difference and redoes the header checksum. Chip RAM is half speed under eight bitplanes: a stock A1200 with fast RAM went from a frozen screen to a running game. recomp/mdamiga: the layer works to a raster deadline with a minimum slice, carries an unfinished picture over the blank and shows it when whole (or after eight blanks), so the game's interrupt comes every frame; colours aren't regrouped while a fade moves

events.title: agk port: sound. The Mega Drive runner has a Z80 (recomp/md/z80.c) running the game's own sound driver, and game --sound-rip DIR plays every request the game can make through it and logs what the YM2612 and the PSG are told. agk/mdsound.py turns that log into Paula's terms: notes with their pitch and level frame by frame, each FM patch rendered per octave to a short looped 8-bit sample by an FM synthesiser in the build, drum samples cut out of the DAC writes, the four most important notes on the four channels, loops found from the notes repeating, and what each request is (music, effect, jingle, stop, fade) read from what it does to music playing. recomp/mdamiga/sound.c plays the stream on a CIA timer and answers the game's writes to its Z80. The ROM bytes only the driver read are blanked and used for samples; the sound goes on a second disk when it doesn't fit. Sonic 2: 28 pieces of music, about 250 effects

events.title: agk port: a Mega Drive game's code rewritten for the Amiga's memory map, checked frame for frame on the host. The analysis run (game --analysis DIR) records coverage, computed-jump targets, the ROM bytes read as data and every instruction that touches hardware; agk port rewrites the code (RAM moved, hardware operands through the layer's cell and calls, pc-relative data made absolute, word pointers brought over, old code turned into jumps to the new) and builds a checking runner (recomp/mdport) that reports anything still reaching for the Mega Drive's addresses; --learn turns that report into hints. Sonic 2: 47379 instructions, 3999 of 4000 frames identical to the original, no stray accesses. docs/genesis-port.md

events.title: recomp: a machine layer. The runtime splits into the shared 68000 + host (recomp/runtime: m68k.h, the interpreter, host.c with the window, PNGs, wav, record/replay, --coverage) and per-machine directories (recomp/amiga, recomp/md); the translation's two code regions come from the machine (bus.h REGION0/1). agk recomp --machine md --rom GAME.md builds a Mega Drive game from its reset vector: the first build interprets everything and gathers its own coverage (game --coverage), the next translates what was played. The Mega Drive chips: VDP (planes, window, sprites, DMA, H/V interrupts, HV counter, scanline rendering), pads, Z80 bus latches; no sound yet. Sonic 2 reaches its title screen.

events.title: Port: the intro made anew for the ST. The fairy and the main menu stay the Amiga programs (FANTASY.S, INTRO.S, common with the Falcon: INTRO_COMMON.S, AMIGA_BLIT.S, the tools in AmbermoonST/port/tools), the intro itself is new (INTRO_ST.S, like Intro.cs): port/tools/intro_st.py makes the file Intro_st with the graphics in the format of the ST screen and the state of every scene per tick (logos, planets, credits, Twinlake, the towns and the meteor, the end screen like the Amiga program). Three screens, the planets, the sun and the meteor scaled at run time, St_sprite (STE blitter or processor) for the fairy and the clouds. The colours of a frame go to the vertical blank before its screen is shown. After the whole intro the song goes on into the menu and its last picture stays until the menu of the Amiga program is there. The music of the intro for the YM2149 (INTRO0.BIN, INTRO1.BIN), the test scenarios start with nointro

events.title: Move the remake's challenges and chapter environment out of the goal window into band badges, follow walking units with the camera, fix the chapter 1 flank tip and animate flanking: the goal window now shows only the win and lose conditions; the challenges become three stars (empty = still open, filled = done, faded = missed) and the environment an icon with its name, in the bottom band left of the 대화 기록 slot in the framed screen (the title cartouche is only 266 wide at the narrowest view and the longest chapter title, 22장 · 신카루스 항구 안, takes 192, so badges there cut titles such as 16장 · 하스가나 사막) and next to the turn plate in the modern bar, where hiding buttons now reserves the title's real width instead of a fixed 120 and the environment badge drops to its icon when that hides fewer buttons; badge widths are measured, not guessed, and the badges get pointer-events back after all: unset (without it real clicks fell through to the map, which a scripted click did not show); clicking a badge opens its window (the challenges with turns left and the best record, or just the environment rule with a help link) and clicking again closes it, opening one closes the other, and the dim extra lines (both sides, see it in the confirm window, stars for what you achieve) are dropped as self-evident; a missed or completed challenge and the last turn of a turn limit show a short toast at the top of the map, and after the opening goal window a band across the map announces the environment once and the badge pulses; tune.json env gets an icon key; walking units push the camera when they come within 1.5 tiles of the map edge, in both editions; in chapter 1 the flank lesson no longer gets lost: surrounding a foe before the counter lesson opens flanking on the spot and its line and card follow that attack, and the turn-start flank introduction no longer counts toward the three tips per battle that used to drop it; on a flanked attack the allies next to the target (up to three) swing too, a beat apart, and 협공 appears on the target (green for us, red for foes); checked in the browser with real clicks in both screen styles, chapters 1, 11, 16 and 24, a 640-wide modern bar and the original edition's camera

events.title: Rewrite the in-battle tip cards and show affinity as icons instead of prose: each card is now one rule sentence, short points for conditions and numbers, and a dim last line only where the screen hint is hard to find, left-aligned, written apart from the help text and cut to what play needs (the user's wording review is applied, e.g. 반격 없음, 처치해야 함, 세 명까지 효과 적용, 방어 선택 시 해당 턴에 피로 회복량 감소, and the promotion card opens with 레벨이 오르면 경우에 따라 무기/방어구를 승급할 수 있습니다); key words are blue because bold does not show in the bitmap font; openWin can measure the real body height (fit) and any window taller than the map now scrolls its body with the buttons kept in view; the hover window drops the weakness/resistance line for trait icons (six races, flying, heavy armour, the six caster elements, new core/affIcons.ts), and the map 휴식 badge and the hover rest forecast go too; the help 약점·내성 table, the affinity card lines, the codex people list and both camp screens and the battle magic list use the same icons (bow, light, dark, wind, water, fire, earth, summon, song, prayer), weaknesses and resistances are green 약점 and red 내성 tags followed by icons, with a drawn green plus for an especially strong weakness, and the help topic gains an icon legend (races not yet met stay hidden) and the three opposite pairs; screen text says 턴 instead of 차례 (help, the mid-battle save notice, the 적 턴 빠르게 setting; character lines keep 차례); the 적도 같음 tag on help topics gives way to a sentence in each topic saying who it applies to (enemies flank only on hard, power and guard are ours only); the 적의 속셈 topic is removed and its alert line moves to 처음이라면, 장 환경 keeps only the confirm-window line and 혼수 only 아무 행동도 할 수 없습니다; the idle opening on the title plays only while the main menu's first screen is showing, not in sub-menus such as settings or difficulty; checked in the browser (cards, a long card scrolling, hover, help, magic list, codex, and idling 67s in settings and the difficulty picker and 75s on the main menu)

last_commit.message: NFS_DOS.EXE of EA's 1997 CD accepted too (a player's: "not the version ReNFS knows"). Its build, dated 17 June 1996, the same 1,254,591 bytes, differs from the 19 June one laid out and relocated only in the give-up branch of keys_control_word 0x48bec (the word written 0x000087a0, not 0xffff87a0; the function 4 bytes longer) and one German text at 0xe3814, neither read by the port: exe.c takes either FNV-1a (0x76078ed2, 0x21ef7c33). With every read checked against those bytes, the 1997 CD drew the same pictures in the front end, the four replays (equal at every snapshot) and nine races. Our CD copy has three bits flipped where the 1997 CD's bytes match their neighbours (NOTES §1). The message no longer says 1996.

before.name: Q8 accelerated-emulation qualification
before.notes: Upstream recommends Q8 only above 20 MHz. v1.8.0 reports Turbo6510 64 MHz measurements on public PAL cube scenes: Mode 2 precise/hybrid 23.70/25.05 FPS, Mode 5 27.00/27.45 FPS, and distant-cube Mode 7 standard/fast/fast+LOD 3.10/6.95/11.50 FPS. These are scene-specific emulator measurements, not minima, general guarantees or physical-hardware qualification. The v1.10.2 stable qualification additionally reports Mode 4 stock/turbo results of 0.649958/30.186113 FPS with defaults and 0.749952/38.484510 FPS with arithmetic, camera and visibility experiments; Mode 7 defaults report 0.044442/3.091013 FPS and arithmetic+UV 0.061107/3.703647 FPS. These remain emulator measurements, not physical-hardware or minimum-machine claims.
